questions.question: Compare a 1:50 000 topographic map with a 1:10 000 orthophoto map.
questions.expected_answer: A 1:50 000 topographic map shows physical and human features with symbols, colours and lines explained in a key, including contour lines, rivers, dams, vegetation, roads, railways, buildings, built-up areas and power lines; 1 cm represents 500 m. South African sheets are numbered by latitude and longitude, for example 2628 for 26 to 27 degrees south and 28 to 29 degrees east. A 1:10 000 orthophoto map is a corrected vertical aerial photograph with contours, names, spot heights, grid and scale added; it shows the real appearance in much more detail at five times the scale, so 1 cm represents 100 m, and covers a smaller area, often outlined on the topographic map. A feature 1 cm long on the topographic map is 5 cm on the orthophoto. Both are read with the title, scale, key, north arrow, grid and date, and are matched using large features such as main roads, railways, rivers or dams.

questions.question: Describe the evidence that identifies the CBD, industrial zones and residential areas on aerial photographs and maps.
questions.expected_answer: The CBD shows the largest and tallest buildings close together with long shadows, little green space, a dense street grid, many vehicles, parking garages and the meeting point of main roads, often with a station or taxi rank; on maps, dense built-up areas, public buildings such as the post office, police station and town hall, and converging roads and railways. Industrial zones show large buildings with big flat or saw-tooth roofs, yards, wide roads and railway sidings, and for heavy industry storage tanks, chimneys, cooling towers, stockpiles and conveyors, often beside a harbour, railway or river and on the edge of the built-up area. High-income residential areas show large plots, big houses, trees, swimming pools, tennis courts, curved streets and cul-de-sacs and possibly golf courses; middle-income areas medium plots in regular streets, townhouses and flats; low-income areas long straight closely spaced rows of small similar houses with few trees and often dirt roads, and informal settlements very dense irregular clusters of small roofs with winding paths, often separated by railways, highways or open land.

questions.question: Explain the claim-evidence-explanation method and use the scale of a 1:10 000 map to find the area of a site measuring 2 cm by 3 cm.
questions.expected_answer: A land use answer should make a claim naming the land use, give at least two pieces of evidence that can actually be seen on the photograph or map, and explain the location using accessibility, land value, the needs of the activity and history; for example, Area B is a high-income area because it has large plots, swimming pools and curved streets, and it is on high ground away from industry where land is attractive and expensive. Errors include giving no evidence, using evidence that cannot be seen, mixing up scales and directions, and confusing a shopping centre with industry instead of using association. On a 1:10 000 map, 1 cm represents 100 m, so 2 cm by 3 cm is 200 m by 300 m, an area of 60 000 square metres, which is 6 hectares since 1 hectare is 10 000 square metres.
